title: To the church that presides
sum: A long greeting, heaped with titles. Ignatius piles title on title for the Roman church: it has received mercy, is loved and given light, 'presides in the region of the Romans', is worthy six times over, is 'presiding over the love', and is 'named after Christ, named after the Father'. Twice he calls Jesus Christ 'our God'. Then he turns to his fear: God has granted his prayer to see them, as a prisoner in chains, and now he is afraid their love will 'do me wrong' by saving him (1:1-2).
Unlike his other letters, this one warns of no false teachers: the Romans are 'filtered clean of every foreign stain'. The only danger he sees in Rome is kindness.
readings: Read as a primacy of honor and love

'Presides' honors the church of the capital, founded on the teaching of Peter and Paul (4:3), and 'the love' is charity: the Roman church is first in rank and first in love (Lightfoot), or holds a place of honor and a 'presidency in love' among the churches (the Orthodox theologian Thomas Hopko).
Read as a witness to Roman primacy

'The love' is the whole fellowship of the churches, over which the Roman church presides: the Second Vatican Council speaks of the Chair of Peter 'which presides over the whole assembly of charity' (Lumen Gentium 13), and the Catechism of the Roman church 'which presides in charity' (Catechism 834).

views.H: Ignatius writes from Smyrna, before reaching Rome (10:1), and he knows the Roman church only by report. 'The region of the Romans' (topos chōriou Rhōmaiōn) is an odd phrase; Lightfoot discusses whether it limits the presidency to a region or locates it, and suggests the doubled noun may be a Syrian way of speaking.
views.N: The greeting's 'mercy' and 'grace' recall Paul's openings, and Paul's letter to the same church praised its faith: 'people are talking about your faith in the whole world' (Romans 1:8). Paul too had longed to see the Roman Christians (Romans 1:11; Romans 15:23).
views.C: The two uses of 'preside' are the place where churches have argued over this letter. See the notes on 'presides in the region of the Romans' and 'presiding over the love', which give Lightfoot's two readings and the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican voices, and the card on Peter and his successors at Matthew 16:18.

deep.b:
Lightfoot first takes 'in the region of the Romans' to give 'the limits over which the supremacy or jurisdiction extends'. He sets aside a reference to the bishops round Rome as 'a great anachronism', 'not to mention that the presidency is here assigned not to the Roman bishop but to the Roman Church', and concludes that the Roman church is 'the principal church in this region, just as the Church of Jerusalem might be said' to preside in the region of the Jews.

'On the other hand it might be urged', he goes on, that the words describe 'not the range of the supremacy, but the locality of the supreme power itself'. Then the verb would speak of 'a certain precedence assigned to the Church of Rome, as situated in the metropolis of the empire and the world, over the other churches of Christendom', 'allied to the "potentior principalitas," which Irenaeus (iii. 3. 2) assigns to the Roman Church; though not so strong in itself'. He rejects it: 'it is difficult to see why Ignatius should write ἐν τόπῳ χωρίου Ῥωμαίων in place of ἐν Ῥώμῃ, which alone would be natural to describe merely the locality. The idea of the "cathedra Petri" therefore has no place here.'

Ignatius uses the same verb of an overseer who 'presides in the place of God' (To the Magnesians 6:1).

deep.title: Claude's theory: presiding by giving
deep.b: Ignatius's only other description of what the Roman church does is that it 'taught others' (3:1) and has never envied anyone. Dionysius of Corinth, some sixty years later, praised Rome's custom of sending help 'to many churches in every city' (Eusebius, Church History 4.23). I suggest that 'presiding over the love' may have struck first readers as a play on that reputation: the church that gives most leads in love. This is my suggestion; it overlaps with Lightfoot's 'first in rank ... first also in love', but goes further in tying the phrase to Rome's giving. The text does not say it.

echoes: Romans 1:7-8; Romans 1:11; Romans 15:23-24; Matthew 16:18; 1 Corinthians 9:21; Matthew 23:24

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch (2:2), a prisoner under guard on the way to execution in Rome
settings.to: The church at Rome, which Ignatius had not yet seen
settings.when: From Smyrna, before he reached Rome (10:1-3), with the Ephesian delegates beside him
settings.why: To win the Romans' goodwill and then turn it: the church with power to help him is asked, out of love, not to use it. Knowing the readers could act changes the tone of the praise; it is a plea as much as a greeting.
settings.readers: The Roman Christians, who the letter assumes could get him freed ('it is easy for you to do what you want', 1:2; 'if you keep silent', 2:1)

title: A word of God, or only a sound
sum: If the Romans keep silent, Ignatius will be 'a word of God'; if they love his flesh, he will be 'only a sound' (2:1). He asks nothing more than to be poured out to God like wine 'while an altar still stands ready', so that they can form a choir and sing because God brought 'the overseer of Syria' from the sunrise to the sunset (2:2).
The chapter gives his one title for himself, and the pictures he keeps returning to: altar, offering, setting and rising.

views.H: 'Overseer of Syria' names him by the province. Eusebius and Jerome make him the second or third bishop of Antioch after Peter (Church History 3.36.2; Lives of Illustrious Men 16).
views.N: Paul's words lie under the chapter: pleasing God, not people (1 Thessalonians 2:4), and 'poured out as a drink offering' (Philippians 2:17; 2 Timothy 4:6).

echoes: 1 Thessalonians 2:4; Galatians 1:10; Philippians 2:17; 2 Timothy 4:6; 1 Clement 5:7; John 1:23

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch (2:2), a prisoner under guard on the way to execution in Rome
settings.to: The church at Rome, which Ignatius had not yet seen
settings.why: To make the Romans' silence an act of worship: if they do nothing, they will have the best deed ever credited to them, and a sacrifice to sing over.

title: Not only called a Christian
sum: The Romans have taught other churches; let what they teach hold good for Ignatius too (3:1). He asks only for strength 'inside and out', so that he may not only be called a Christian but be found one, and be faithful 'when the world no longer sees me' (3:2). Nothing seen is good; Christ, now with the Father, is seen more than ever; Christianity is 'not a work of persuading but of greatness, when the world hates it' (3:3).

views.H: The noun 'Christianity' (3:3) is not in the New Testament; Ignatius uses it here, in To the Magnesians 10 and in To the Philadelphians 6. Lake notes that 3:3 is 'clumsily expressed' for the sake of a play on words.
views.N: The New Testament's three uses of 'Christian' (Acts 11:26; Acts 26:28; 1 Peter 4:16) and Paul's seen and unseen (2 Corinthians 4:18) are the background.

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch (2:2), a prisoner under guard on the way to execution in Rome
settings.to: The church at Rome, which Ignatius had not yet seen
settings.why: To turn the Romans from action to prayer: the only help he wants from them is prayer for courage.

title: God's wheat
sum: The center of the letter. Ignatius has written to all the churches that he dies for God willingly, 'if you do not stop me'. 'I am God's wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts so that I may be found pure bread of Christ' (4:1). Let the beasts be his tomb, so that no one must bury him; then he will truly be a disciple (4:2). He does not command them as Peter and Paul did: they were apostles and free, he is a condemned man and a slave, but in death he will be Christ's freed person (4:3).
This is the line ancient readers quoted: Irenaeus, Eusebius and Jerome all give it.

views.H: Irenaeus quotes 4:1 about AD 180 without naming Ignatius, 'one of ours' (Against Heresies 5.28.4); Eusebius quotes Irenaeus's Greek (Church History 3.36.12). The Catholic Encyclopedia says that with this passage 'the evidence of authenticity becomes compelling'. The wording of the last words differs among the witnesses (see the variant).
views.N: Peter and Paul as the apostles of the Roman church (4:3), the free man and the apostle of 1 Corinthians 9:1, the freed person of 1 Corinthians 7:22, the grain of wheat of John 12:24.
views.C: 'Pure bread' and the later 'God's bread' (7:3) bring the church's thanksgiving meal to mind; see the views note at 7:3. On seeking martyrdom see the views note at 4:1.

deep.b: Irenaeus, in Gaul about 180, writes that tribulation grinds the saved like wheat for the royal banquet, and adds a saying. His Greek, which Eusebius preserves, reads: 'as one of ours said, condemned to the beasts because of his witness toward God: "I am God's wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts, so that I may be found pure bread"' (Against Heresies 5.28.4; Church History 3.36.12). The Latin translation of Irenaeus, as Lightfoot reports it, has 'wheat of Christ' and 'bread of God'. Jerome's Latin adds a scene: when Ignatius heard the lions roaring (cum rugientes audiret leones), he said Frumentum Christi sum, 'I am Christ's wheat', ending 'so that I may be found pure bread' (Lives of Illustrious Men 16). The Orthodox Church in America's life puts the saying in his mouth in the arena. So the sentence was known to Irenaeus in Gaul within about seventy years, and later to Eusebius and Jerome.

echoes: John 12:24; 1 Corinthians 10:17; 1 Corinthians 9:1; 1 Corinthians 7:22; Romans 12:1; 1 Clement 5:4-7

settings.what: Let me be food for beasts
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch (2:2), a prisoner under guard on the way to execution in Rome
settings.to: The church at Rome, which Ignatius had not yet seen
settings.when: The heart of the plea, after his request for prayer
settings.why: To make the Romans see his death as he sees it: an offering that turns him into bread, the moment he becomes a true disciple and a free man. 4:3 also guards against seeming to command them: he asks; the apostles commanded.

title: Ten leopards
sum: From Syria to Rome, by land and sea, by night and day, Ignatius is 'fighting wild beasts': ten soldiers, 'leopards', who only get worse when treated well (5:1). He longs for the real beasts, will coax them to be quick, and will force them if they hold back (5:2). 'Now I am beginning to be a disciple.' Let fire, cross, beasts, the tearing of the body and the devil's tortures come, 'only let me reach Jesus Christ' (5:3).
Eusebius quotes 5:1-3, with small differences, as his proof of the letter.

views.H: Eusebius gives 5:1-3, introducing it as 'word for word' though his Greek lacks two items of the list (Church History 3.36.7-9; see the variant at 5:3), and Jerome a Latin form of it (Lives of Illustrious Men 16). Lake: 'leopard' here is 'the first instance of the word' in Greek or Latin literature.
views.N: 'I fought with wild beasts at Ephesus' (1 Corinthians 15:32) and 'I am not justified by that' (1 Corinthians 4:4) are in Lake's margin.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 15:32; 1 Corinthians 4:4; Romans 8:35-39; Luke 14:27; Martyrdom of Polycarp 3:1

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch (2:2), a prisoner under guard on the way to execution in Rome
settings.to: The church at Rome, which Ignatius had not yet seen
settings.when: On the road, from Syria to Smyrna so far
settings.why: To show the Romans that he is already suffering and does not shrink: the worse it gets, the more he becomes a disciple. The list of tortures answers any fear they may have for him.

title: My birth is upon me
sum: The ends of the earth and the kingdoms of this age will do him no good; it is better to die into Christ Jesus than to be king of the world. 'I am looking for him who died for us.' His birth is upon him (6:1). 'Do not keep me from living. Do not want me to die': to save his body would be to keep him from life. Let him receive pure light; there he will become a human being (6:2). Let him imitate 'the suffering of my God' (6:3).

views.N: Jesus's question about winning the whole world (Matthew 16:26) and Paul's 'living is Christ and dying is gain' (Philippians 1:21) stand behind the chapter; Lake's margin gives 1 Corinthians 9:15.
views.C: 'The suffering of my God' (6:3) is the kind of phrase later churches defended and explained: the Son of God suffered in the flesh. See the topic on the Trinity.

echoes: Matthew 16:26; Matthew 4:8; 1 Corinthians 9:15; Philippians 1:21-23; John 16:21; 1 Corinthians 11:1

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch (2:2), a prisoner under guard on the way to execution in Rome
settings.to: The church at Rome, which Ignatius had not yet seen
settings.why: To turn the Romans' idea of life and death upside down, so that letting him die becomes the loving thing.

title: Living water, God's bread
sum: 'The ruler of this age' wants to snatch Ignatius away, so let no one in Rome help him (7:1). Even if Ignatius himself begs them in person, they should trust this letter instead. 'My love has been crucified'; no fire for material things is left, only living water that says inside him, 'Come to the Father' (7:2). He wants no food that decays, but 'God's bread, which is the flesh of Jesus Christ', and for drink 'his blood, which is love that does not decay' (7:3).
The bread and the blood of 7:3 are read in more than one way: see the views note.
readings: Read as union with Christ through death

Lightfoot: the reference 'is not to the eucharist itself but to the union with Christ which is symbolized and pledged in the eucharist', the union Ignatius expects to complete through martyrdom; the reference to the bread and cup is indirect, 'analogous to that which our Lord makes in John vi'.
Read with a reference to the church's meal

Zahn, as Lightfoot reports him, finds in 'love that does not decay' a secondary reference to the love-feast of which the thanksgiving formed a part; Lake's footnote suggests a play on agapē as a name for the church's meal. Ignatius's language elsewhere (Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 7:1) speaks of the thanksgiving directly.

views.H: Lightfoot's notes show the text of 7:2 was confused in the witnesses (see the variant). Origen, a century later, quoted 'my love is crucified' and took 'my love' to mean Christ (as Lightfoot quotes him).
views.N: John's Gospel is everywhere: living water (John 4:10; John 7:38), God's bread (John 6:33), flesh and blood (John 6:51-58), David's seed (John 7:42), and 'the world's ruler' (John 14:30).
views.C: On how the churches understand Christ's presence in the Supper see the views note at 7:3 and the cards at Matthew 26:26 and John 6:53-58.

deep.b: Lightfoot takes erōs in its usual sense, 'my earthly passion': the word means sensual passion in its only two uses in the Greek Old Testament, and the New Testament avoids it. 'His ἀγάπη, we might say, was perfected, when his ἔρως was crucified.' Origen, in the prologue to his Commentary on the Song of Songs, as Lightfoot quotes it, remembered 'one of the saints, Ignatius by name', who said of Christ 'My Love is crucified', and used it to defend calling God 'Love' (amor, erōs) as John calls him agapē (1 John 4:8). Lightfoot calls Origen's reading 'a wholly different interpretation', followed by Pseudo-Dionysius and others. Both readings fit Ignatius's mind: the first matches 'no fire ... that loves material things' in the same verse; the second matches his longing for Christ in 6:1.

echoes: John 4:10; John 4:14; John 7:38-39; John 6:33; John 6:51-58; John 7:42; Romans 1:3; 2 Timothy 2:8; Galatians 5:24; John 14:30; 1 Corinthians 2:6-8

settings.what: The ruler of this age and God's bread
settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch (2:2), a prisoner under guard on the way to execution in Rome
settings.to: The church at Rome, which Ignatius had not yet seen
settings.why: To warn that the wish to save him serves the devil, and to show the Romans what he hungers for instead. 'Do not be won over by me' even in person: he foresees his own courage failing and asks them to hold him to this letter.

title: Believe me
sum: Ignatius no longer wants to live as people do. If the Romans want it, it will happen: 'Want it, so that you too may be wanted' (8:1). He asks them, in these few lines, to believe him; Jesus Christ, 'the mouth that does not lie', will show them he is telling the truth (8:2). If he suffers, it will be their kindness; if he is turned away, their hatred (8:3).

views.N: Christ as the Father's truthful mouth recalls John's Word (John 1:18) and 'the witness who is faithful and true' (Revelation 3:14).

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch (2:2), a prisoner under guard on the way to execution in Rome
settings.to: The church at Rome, which Ignatius had not yet seen
settings.why: To leave the Romans no room for doubt that he means what he says.

title: The church in Syria
sum: Ignatius asks the Romans to pray for the church in Syria, which now has God as its shepherd in his place: 'Jesus Christ alone will oversee it, along with your love' (9:1). He is ashamed to be counted one of its members, 'the last of them and one born at the wrong time', Paul's words for himself (9:2). The churches along his road have welcomed him and gone ahead of him city by city (9:3).

views.H: Lake names, among the motives he finds in Ignatius's letters ('all or some of which can be traced in each letter'), his wish 'to secure the future of his own church in Antioch by persuading other communities to send helpers'. In this letter he asks only for prayer.
views.N: 1 Corinthians 15:8-9 (Lake's margin) gives 'one born at the wrong time' and 'the least'; 1 Peter 2:25 calls Christ the 'Overseer' of souls.

echoes: 1 Corinthians 15:8-9; 1 Peter 2:25; 1 Peter 5:4; Ephesians 3:8; Polycarp to the Philippians 1:1

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch (2:2), a prisoner under guard on the way to execution in Rome
settings.to: The church at Rome, which Ignatius had not yet seen
settings.why: To hand his church to the Romans' prayers and to Christ, and to show the Romans the welcome other churches have given him.

title: From Smyrna, 24 August
sum: Ignatius writes from Smyrna, 'by the Ephesians', with Crocus and many others beside him (10:1). Some Syrians have gone ahead to Rome; tell them he is near (10:2). He dates the letter 'the ninth day before the Kalends of September', 24 August as Lake renders it, and says farewell 'in the endurance of Jesus Christ' (10:3).

views.H: The letter is dated by day and month. No year is given; Eusebius's Chronicle puts the martyrdom in the tenth year of Trajan (Lake gives AD 108), Jerome in the eleventh.

settings.by: Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch (2:2), a prisoner under guard on the way to execution in Rome
settings.to: The church at Rome, which Ignatius had not yet seen
settings.why: To place the letter and ask a kindness for those who went ahead of him.
settings.readers: The Roman church, and the Syrian Christians already in Rome (10:2), whom Ignatius commends to them
